cards.title: Characterizing sub-base-two algorithms for symmetric Boolean CSPs
cards.formal: Characterize the possibly infinite symmetric Boolean constraint languages Γ for which one common constant 1≤c_Γ<2 works as an exponential running-time base for every finite sublanguage Γ′⊆Γ, allowing the algorithm to depend on Γ′. The source permits a non-uniform characterization and conditional lower bounds, but does not fix a single proposed characterization or final hardness convention.
cards.why: Would identify which local counting constraints permit a uniform exponential improvement over enumerating all Boolean assignments. The common-base requirement distinguishes a structural tractability principle from speedups that vanish as the allowed constraint family expands.
cards.status_note: Workshop formulation and the referenced non-uniform model recovered; subsequent searches through 11 September 2026 found no matching general classification. The proposed classification and final conditional/randomized conventions remain unspecified in the source.

sentences: Each constraint accepts a Boolean tuple according to how many of its argument occurrences are one.
The question asks which possibly infinite families of such constraints admit a common exponential running-time base below two.
An algorithm may depend on a finite sublanguage, but the improved base must work for every finite sublanguage of the chosen family.
Separate fixed-arity speedups whose bases approach two do not meet this requirement.
The source asks for a general classification and still leaves its precise proposed criterion and hardness conventions to be fixed.

cards.definitions: For arity r≥1 and a set S⊆{0,…,r}, define R_(r,S)={(b₁,…,b_r)∈{0,1}^r:∑ᵢbᵢ∈S}. A symmetric Boolean language Γ is a set of such relations, possibly of unbounded arity. A finite CSP(Γ′) instance has n Boolean variables and a finite list of constraints R(x₁,…,x_r) with R∈Γ′; variable indices may repeat, and each occurrence contributes to the sum. A satisfying assignment meets every constraint. Each finite Γ′ is fixed for its algorithm, so relations can have fixed names and their truth tables can be built into that algorithm. If N is the length of the explicit variable-and-constraint input, an O*(cⁿ) bound permits a polynomial factor N^k. Following the cited paper, the non-uniform improvement property is ∃c_Γ∈[1,2) ∀finite Γ′⊆Γ ∃algorithm A_Γ′ solving CSP(Γ′) in O*(c_Γⁿ) time. The algorithm, polynomial exponent and multiplicative constant may depend on Γ′; the exponential base may not. This use of non-uniform does not mean arbitrary advice depending on the input length. Symmetry here means invariance under permutation of argument positions; it does not automatically permit negated variables or impose closure of Γ under negation. The source mentions the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis as a possible lower-bound premise: for every δ>0, some fixed k has no O*((2−δ)ⁿ)-time algorithm for k-CNF satisfiability, in the chosen deterministic or randomized convention. That convention and the requested form of characterization remain to be finalized.
cards.answer_criterion: State a precise characterization of the languages with the common-base property, prove its sufficiency by algorithms and its necessity under an explicitly fixed permitted hardness premise. The final benchmark still needs a selected proposed equivalence or a specified representation and classification task. Separate bounds c_Γ′<2 that approach 2 over larger finite sublanguages do not establish one common c_Γ<2.

context_blocks.title: A constraint sees only the number of ones
context_blocks.text: For r=3 and S={1}, a constraint requires exactly one of its three argument occurrences to be one. For S={1,2,3}, it requires at least one one. Permuting positions preserves these relations, but different constraints can overlap on variables and impose competing requirements.

context_blocks.title: The same saving must survive larger sublanguages
context_blocks.text: For illustration, a sequence of bases 2−1/r is below two for every fixed r, but has no common upper bound strictly below two as r grows. The source’s non-uniform model requires a single exponential saving for the whole language, even though each finite fragment may use a different algorithm.

context_blocks.title: Two notions of symmetry should not be conflated
context_blocks.text: The earlier paper studies sign-symmetric languages, meaning closure under certain negation and partial-assignment operations. The workshop instead requires each relation to depend only on its number of ones. These are different conditions, so results for one class cannot be transferred merely because both names contain symmetric.

context_blocks.title: The target is a boundary across languages
context_blocks.text: The workshop asks which symmetric languages admit the common-base improvement, with lower bounds potentially based on SETH. Its separate Sidon-set question is one restricted case. The general classification is preserved here rather than replaced by that restriction.

notes: Recovered symmetric relations, possibly infinite languages and the common-base quantifier order.
statement_review.remaining_issue: The actual symmetry and non-uniform speedup property are recovered. The source asks for a characterization of all possibly infinite languages, permits non-uniform algorithms, and offers SETH only as an example of an allowed lower-bound premise. It does not fix a single proposed characterization, a representation on which that characterization must be decidable, or the precise admissible randomized/conditional lower-bound conventions. A complete yes/no benchmark requires those choices, without replacing the general classification by the separate Sidon-set question.

cards.context:
For r=3 and S={1}, a constraint requires exactly one of its three argument occurrences to be one. For S={1,2,3}, it requires at least one one. Permuting positions preserves these relations, but different constraints can overlap on variables and impose competing requirements.

For illustration, a sequence of bases 2−1/r is below two for every fixed r, but has no common upper bound strictly below two as r grows. The source’s non-uniform model requires a single exponential saving for the whole language, even though each finite fragment may use a different algorithm.

The earlier paper studies sign-symmetric languages, meaning closure under certain negation and partial-assignment operations. The workshop instead requires each relation to depend only on its number of ones. These are different conditions, so results for one class cannot be transferred merely because both names contain symmetric.

The workshop asks which symmetric languages admit the common-base improvement, with lower bounds potentially based on SETH. Its separate Sidon-set question is one restricted case. The general classification is preserved here rather than replaced by that restriction.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
